# Introduction

Melt of the seasonal snowpack directly supports over two billion people worldwide by sustaining downstream ecosystems, energy production, and agricultural irrigation [@Immerzeel2020; @Viviroli2020; @Mankin2015]. The high albedo and energy required to melt snow also provides a large-scale cooling effect for the Earth by reflecting most of the incoming solar radiation and dissipating energy during spring melt [@Male1980; @Henderson2018; @Leach2014]. Snow falls in forested areas over 50% of the northern hemisphere [@Kim2017], and over 20% of the global landmass [@Deschamps-Berger2025]. Intercepted snow in the canopy is subjected to higher rates of sublimation and melt compared to the subcanopy snowpack due to greater surface area, turbulent energy exchange, and solar exposure [@Storck2002; @Pomeroy1998b]. In cold-dry continental climates, researchers estimate that 25 to 60% of annual snowfall may be lost to the sublimation of intercepted snow from the canopy [@Essery2003; @Sanmiguel-Vallelado2017;@Pomeroy1995; @Ellis2010]. In warm-humid maritime climates the majority of snowfall melts in the canopy [@Storck2002; @Floyd2012], limiting atmospheric losses from sublimation, and contributes to changes in the phase and timing of precipitation reaching the ground. The strong hydrological influence of forest canopies on snowfall partitioning leads to high variability of snowpack accumulation in forested basins [@Rojas-Heredia2024; @Staines2023; @Mazzotti2021; @Moeser2015]. Observations of this variability are sparse and unrepresentative due to instrumented stations being primarily located in clearing and low elevations [@Vionnet2021]. Moreover, observing snow accumulation under forest canopies over large extents remains uncertain with current remote sensing methodologies [@Rittger2020]. Therefore, accurately diagnosing the effects of climate and vegetation change on snowpack accumulation requires models capable of representing snow interception and redistribution processes within forested environments.

Limited observations of processes governing snowfall partitioning by forest canopies—including throughfall, interception, and the subsequent unloading, wind redistribution, sublimation, drip, and melt of intercepted snow—have led to uncertainties in representing these processes in hydrological models [@Lundquist2021]. Existing snow interception parameterisations have been developed for both warm maritime [@Storck2002; @Andreadis2009] and cold continental [@Hedstrom1998; @Ellis2010; @Roesch2001] climates characterized by dense forest canopy. The strong dependence of snowfall partitioning by vegetation on meteorology and canopy density [@Hedstrom1998; @Storck2002] has led to differing process emergence in these two distinct climates and forest types and uncertain transferability to new regions [@Lundquist2021; @Lumbrazo2022]. In addition to climate-driven process differences, variability in the measurements used to develop existing theories of snow interception and canopy snow ablation—and uncertainty regarding which processes these measurements capture—leads to differences in the processes represented in current models. As a result, these parameterisations often need to be calibrated when applied to new regions to better represent local interception processes [e.g., @Lumbrazo2022]. Although satisfactory model performance in simulating subcanopy snow water equivalent (SWE) has been achieved across different climates in some studies [@Essery2004; @Gelfan2004], other snow model comparisons [@Krinner2018; @Rutter2009] have shown limited performance. Limited testing of these theories under varying canopy densities and meteorological conditions has created uncertainty about their applicability across different climates and forest types. 

In hydrological models, partitioning of snowfall in forest canopies is typically handled by first calculating the fraction of snowfall that is intercepted in the canopy (initial interception) and then using parameterisations for ablation processes including unloading, melt/drip, and sublimation [@Ellis2010; @Clark2015; @Pomeroy2022]. @Lundquist2021 and @Staines2023 show that parameterisations developed by @Hedstrom1998 and @Storck2002, which are commonly used in hydrological and land surface models [@Clark2015; @Pomeroy2022; @Verseghy2017], may overemphasize the effect of canopy snow load and/or air temperature on throughfall during the initial interception process. New observations of initial interception that minimize the inclusion of subsequent canopy snow ablation processes could help determine if existing relationships are generally applicable across a wide range of meteorological conditions. Advances in aerial LiDAR (light detection and ranging) technologies have enabled the creation of highly detailed canopy models [@Staines2023; @Moeser2015]; however, so far, measurements of the interception process at comparable resolutions remain limited to a single site [@Staines2023]. Moreover, the theory proposed by @Hedstrom1998 to represent variability in initial interception based on snowfall trajectory angle has not yet been validated, and new LiDAR-derived canopy models offer the potential to do so. Additional observations spanning both meteorological and canopy density gradients would improve assessment of the applicability of existing theories to represent the initial interception process across diverse climates and forest types.

The importance of representing both dry/cold- and melt-induced unloading of snow in the canopy has been shown in several studies [@Gelfan2004; @Essery2004; @Roesch2001; @Ellis2010]. These processes are supported through physical mechanisms such as loss of structural integrity, particle bond weakening, and lubrication of intercepted snow during the melt process [@Storck2002; @Floyd2012]. Sublimation has been proposed to promote unloading via structural degradation and bond weakening of intercepted snow [@MacDonald2010]. Wind drag promotes unloading through shear stress applied to intercepted snow, wind erosion through direct entrainment in the atmosphere of intercepted snow, and branch movement [@Roesch2001; @Bartlett2015; @Lumbrazo2022]. Increasing air temperature promotes unloading by increasing the elasticity of branches and its direct effect on enthalpy and hence melt and/or sublimation [@Schmidt1990; @Schmidt1991]. While direct measurements of canopy snow unloading associated with melt were provided by @Storck2002 from a warm maritime climate using detailed process-level lysimetry, dry-snow unloading parameterisations have been developed from indirect measurements of above-canopy albedo, which may overestimate unloading because they also capture other ablation processes such as sublimation and melt [@Roesch2001; @Bartlett2015]. Therefore, validation of the theories underlying dry-snow unloading parameterisations would benefit from additional direct observations of canopy snow unloading that are less likely to mix other processes compared to previous indirect measurements. Moreover, the canopy snowmelt induced unloading association proposed by @Storck2002 was based on a single event in a coastal climate and thus should be validated using additional observations across differing meteorologies and canopy snow loads. Additional processes not currently represented in snow interception models—including wind redistribution of snow, rain on intercepted snow, ice deposition, and the cohesion and adhesion of snow within the canopy—should be investigated to assess their relative importance and potential emergence at new sites.

Future climate change is expected to change the dominant hydrological processes in forested basins as a result of the dependence of many hydrological processes on temperature, precipitation, and vegetation structure [@He2021; @He2023; @Dettinger2014; @Viviroli2011; @Fang2020b]. A report by Environment and Climate Change Canada [@Bush2019], suggest an increase in Canadian mean annual air temperature of 2 °C from the 1986-2005 reference period by 2050 for the low emission scenario and 6 °C for the high emission scenario by the late 21^st^ century. @Bush2019 project an increase in annual mean precipitation over all of Canada during the second half of the 21^st^ century, with a larger increase in northern Canada. As the climate warms, forest regions across Canada are expected to experience a shift in snow interception processes. For example, continental climates in Canada may shift from a dry-snow unloading and sublimation dominated regime to one characterized by increased canopy snowmelt and drip, altering the net snow accumulation in these areas. However, the limited transferability of existing parameterisations to represent this shift across differing environments makes accurate predictions of these projected changes uncertain. In addition to climate-driven shifts in snow processes, vegetation cover is already changing due to drought [@Dai2013], disease [@Ruess2021], insect outbreaks [@Kurz2008], fire [@Kasischke2006; @Kasischke2010], land-use change [@Lopez-Moreno2014], and shifts in species composition [@Gottfried2012]. These changes in temperature, precipitation, and forest structure, species, and density are expected to strongly influence snowpack accumulation worldwide. Thus, further investigation into the theories underlying existing snow interception and canopy snow ablation parameterisations is warranted to ensure models of these processes are robust across diverse climates and forest canopies for understanding potential future changes in snow hydrology worldwide.

To assess the performance of parameterisations to represent snowfall partitioning by interception in needleleaf canopies, a modular and flexible model platform will be used to simulate the individual mass and energy balance fluxes and states of the canopy and snowpack. The advantage of modular and flexible model platforms is that it is possible to adjust process parameterisations while holding the remaining model parameters and mass and energy conservation equations constant [@Pomeroy2007; @Clark2015]. The Cold Regions Hydrological Model platform [CRHM, @Pomeroy2022] will be used in this study as its mass and energy balance parameterisations have been successfully used in previous studies [@Ellis2010; @Pomeroy2012; @Rasouli2019b; @Sanmiguel2022] to assess forest-snow interactions in Spain, USA, and Canada. Since CRHM is a process-based model agnostic platform, individual state and flux variables including subcanopy snow accumulation, snow interception, sublimation, unloading, drip, and wind redistribution can be evaluated using differing parameterisations. To evaluate existing parameterisations of snow interception [@Hedstrom1998;@Storck2002;@Andreadis2009], and ablation of canopy snow by unloading [@Ellis2010; @Roesch2001; @Andreadis2009], drip [@Storck2002;@Andreadis2009; @Ellis2010] and sublimation [@Pomeroy1998b], CRHM will be run at four mountain forest research basins in western and northern Canada and compared to in-situ observations of subcanopy SWE. Modifications to the existing parameterisations to improve representation of snow interception processes based on field investigations at a well instrumented subalpine forest in the Canadian Rockies will be validated on the associated change in error in simulated and observed forest snow accumulation and other interception processes where measured.

## Research Objectives

The overarching goal of this thesis is to better understand the dominant processes that govern snowfall partitioning through interception in needleleaf forest canopies and to determine how these processes can be accurately represented in hydrological models suitable for application across a range of climate and forest types. To achieve this goal, two specific research objectives were formulated each with underlying research question(s):

### Objective 1: Evaluate the suitability of existing snow interception and ablation parameterisations for application in needleleaf forests with differing canopy structure and meteorology.

1. What are the theoretical underpinnings and assumptions underpinning existing snow interception and ablation parameterisations?  
   
2. Are the theories and assumptions of existing snow interception parameterisations supported by field measurements collected across diverse canopy structures and meteorological conditions?  
   
3. Are the theories and assumptions of existing canopy snow ablation parameterisations supported by field measurements collected across varying meteorological conditions?

### Objective 2: Determine how new snow interception and ablation parameterisations could enhance the representation of processes important for subcanopy snow accumulation. 

4. How can the use of novel snow interception parameterisations enhance simulations of snow accumulation in forests with differing tree species, canopy structures, and meteorological conditions?

## Organization of Chapters

Following the Introduction of the thesis (Chapter 1), four manuscripts are presented as thesis chapters designed for submission to peer-reviewed journals and correspond to the aforementioned four research questions. Chapter 2 addresses Research Question 1 by providing a comprehensive review of the literature on snow interception and ablation parameterisations. This review identified the theories and assumptions underlying existing parameterisations and highlights the primary research gaps that this thesis seeks to address. The outcomes of Chapter 2 provide the foundation for evaluating parameterisations using field observations in the subsequent chapters.

Chapter 3 addresses Research Question 2 by presenting an evaluation of snow interception relationships based on novel observations of throughfall and canopy density. The results demonstrate theories underlying existing snow interception parameterisations are not supported and show improved representation of the initial interception process across diverse meteorology, snow loads, and canopy densities is possible with a new parameterisation.

Chapter 4 addresses Research Question 3 through an evaluation of processes regarding canopy snow ablation processes using a hybrid diagnostic mass balance approach which combined both direct observations of individual canopy snow ablation processes with simulations where some process observations were not available (i.e., canopy snow sublimation). The results reveal that canopy snow load, wind shear stress, and snowmelt were most strongly associated with unloading and differed from existing theories. These findings highlight the need for comprehensive physically based parameterisations to accurately represent canopy snow ablation. Collectively, Chapters 2 through 4 demonstrate the successful completion of Objective 1.

Chapter 5 addresses Objective 2 (and Research Question 4) and describes the development of a new canopy snow model that incorporates the relationships identified in Chapters 3 and 4. The model is implemented in the Cold Regions Hydrological Modelling Platform across four research sites in western and northern Canada. Results demonstrate improved simulations of subcanopy SWE, especially under warm-humid climates dominated by canopy snow melt, validating the new parameterisations.

The thesis concludes with Chapter 6 which provides a synthesis of the results and conclusions from the previous chapters.
